evidence_set: After repeated nightly dosing, flurazepam was worse than placebo, SMD 1.65 (95% CI 0.98 to 2.32; k = 9, n = 806), and was outperformed by all other compounds.

In on-road tests in the morning or afternoon after one or two nights of bedtime use, the most severe residual effects were found for flurazepam and loprazolam at their higher doses, worse than with a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 g/L; nitrazepam, flunitrazepam and lormetazepam (capsules) at their higher doses, flurazepam at the lower dose, oxazepam and zopiclone were equivalent to 0.5 to 0.8 g/L; lormetazepam (lower dose, capsules), temazepam soft capsules and nitrazepam at the lower dose had no significant residual effects.

In a second test in the afternoon, impairment declined rapidly for the short- and intermediate-acting zopiclone, lormetazepam (higher dose) and oxazepam but remained or increased for the long-acting flunitrazepam and nitrazepam (higher doses).

evidence_set: Across the performance tests the treatment effect was only a trend, F(7,65) = 1.98, P < 0.07; practice effects across trials and days were significant (P < 0.001).

No significant group effects on individual performance tests, although trial-by-group interactions were significant for digit-symbol substitution and reaction time; pairwise digit-symbol differences: on day 1 caffeine after a placebo night beat placebo-placebo, and on day 2 higher-dose flurazepam with morning placebo scored below lower-dose flurazepam, higher-dose flurazepam with caffeine and lower-dose triazolam; no significant group effects on mood (POMS or visual analogue mood).

80 healthy young male volunteers, non-smokers with a capped usual caffeine intake (threshold on the study card), good sleepers, randomly assigned in equal numbers to eight double-blind groups; no caffeinated beverages allowed during the 2.5 days in the laboratory.

evidence_set: In a UK case-crossover study of 19 386 drivers in a first traffic accident, comparing each driver's periods with and without exposure, the odds ratio was 1.2 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics and 2.2 (1.5 to 3.1) for anxiolytic benzodiazepines; zopiclone, the only short half-life hypnotic, had an odds ratio of 4.0.

In a nested case-control study of drivers aged 65 or over (5579 injurious crashes, 13 256 controls), odds ratios were 1.0 (0.8 to 1.3) for benzodiazepines with half-lives of 24 hours or less and 1.5 (1.0 to 2.0) for longer ones in week 1 of use; in a matched case-control study of older drivers (234 injurious crashes, 447 controls), 0.9 (0.4 to 2.0) for benzodiazepines, mostly flurazepam and triazolam.

Risks of fall-related injury were highest at the start of treatment: odds ratio 3.6 in the first two weeks, 2.3 in weeks 3 and 4 and 1.4 in the second month after a hypnotic prescription; in nursing-home residents using benzodiazepines, adjusted rate ratios for falls of 3.0 in week 1, 2.2 in weeks 2 to 4 and 1.3 in the second month.

The authors suggest that repeated administration seemed to reduce residual effects, likely through tolerance, except for flurazepam, whose effects may need more time to build tolerance.
